summary:
OrbitWatch is an accessible, zero-install citizen science web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to identify moving celestial bodieslike asteroids, brown dwarfs, and hypothetical Planet X candidatesin multi-epoch infrared sky survey data like NASA's SPHEREx.

The problem of combing through vast all-sky surveys takes orbiting the system by eye, OrbitWatch offers visualization tools: animated blinking, difference imaging, and interactive wipe comparisons. An automated multi-variable scoring algorithm takes care of candidate triage, weighing proper motion against signal-to-noise and detector artefact risk. Mariner in simulators, or pull in real NASA/IPAC and JPL Small-Body NASA/IRSA cutouts, enter structured verdicts, and output verifiable evidence notes with direct links to official NASA/IPAC and JPL SSDB logs.

Why OrbitWatch Matters To confirm the presence of objects in the faint and outer reaches of the solar system we need to distinguish authentic astronomical motion from sensor artifacts. OrbitWatch's combination of algorithmic scoring with the human-eye and scientific vigilance (a change is a lead, not a discovery) brings discovery to the hands of the many, not just a few.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

OrbitWatch is an interactive, browser-based celestial inspection platform and candidate evaluation tool inspired by the historic blink comparator technique (the method Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930), modernized for NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission.

  • Multi-Epoch Inspection Suite: Users compare observations of identical coordinates across different observation epochs using four visualization modes:
    • ▶ Blink: Automatically flips between the earlier and later observation to reveal shifting objects.
    • Date Slider: Lets the user smoothly scrub back and forth across time.
    • Show Difference: Generates an optical difference map highlighting earlier positions in pink and later positions in blue, while isolated glowing markers reveal flux/brightness variability.
    • ↔ Compare (Wipe): A draggable before-and-after curtain divider that allows direct side-by-side verification.
  • Transparent Multi-Factor Scoring Algorithm: Evaluates potential candidates through a dynamic formula balancing four core metrics (0–100): Score=max⁡(0,Motion⋅w1+Signal Clarity⋅w2+Cross-Catalog Match⋅w3−Artifact Risk⋅w4w1+w2+w3+w4)\text{Score} = \max\left(0, \frac{\text{Motion} \cdot w_1 + \text{Signal Clarity} \cdot w_2 + \text{Cross-Catalog Match} \cdot w_3 - \text{Artifact Risk} \cdot w_4}{w_1 + w_2 + w_3 + w_4}\right)Score=max(0,w1​+w2​+w3​+w4​Motion⋅w1​+Signal Clarity⋅w2​+Cross-Catalog Match⋅w3​−Artifact Risk⋅w4​​) Users can adjust the default weights (35,30,20,1535, 30, 20, 1535,30,20,15) in real time to test different survey hypotheses.
  • Candidate Queue & Human-in-the-Loop Verdicts: Users can review ranked leads, log verdicts (Likely Real Motion, Likely Image Problem, or Needs Follow-Up) saved locally to the browser, and click Copy Evidence Note to generate a formatted citation report.
  • Real NASA Data Integration: Includes an astronomical coordinate calculator linking directly to the official NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SPHEREx Data Explorer, alongside a local image loader allowing users to import two aligned FITS/PNG cutouts into the browser viewer.
  • "Spot the Mover" Educational Mini-Game: An interactive learning module that trains users' visual perception to identify shifting pixels against crowded starfields.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Friction Accessibility: Runs directly from a single index.html file in any modern browser. Requires no installation, account registration, external server setup, or API keys.
  • Elimination of False Positives: Automated difference pipelines often get fooled by diffraction spikes, cosmic ray hits, optical ghosts, and bad detector pixels. Pairing automated triage with human visual inspection drastically weeds out sensor artifacts.
  • Explainable & Transparent: Replaces opaque "black box" machine learning models with a clear, user-tunable scoring engine and plain-language candidate explanations.
  • Privacy & Client-Side Autonomy: User-uploaded astronomical cutouts are rendered entirely in the browser memory using the HTML5 File API and Canvas, without transmitting data to external servers. Review verdicts persist safely on the device via localStorage.
  • Universal Design: Fully responsive from desktop to mobile screens, with accessible ARIA tab roles, keyboard navigation, high-contrast visual indicators, and prefers-reduced-motion compliance.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Democratizing Astronomical Discovery: Bridges the gap between complex multi-terabyte astronomical archives (IRSA/SPHEREx) and citizen scientists, students, and amateur astronomers worldwide.
  • Promoting Scientific Integrity: Instills the core operational principle: "A change is a lead, not a discovery." OrbitWatch avoids sensationalized "Planet X discovered!" claims, instead enforcing rigorous evidence documentation and verification against existing catalogs.
  • Accelerating Professional Follow-Up: Pre-filters and formats standardized evidence dossiers (including RA/Dec coordinates, epoch timestamps, motion vectors, and artifact checks) that professional observatories and survey teams can rapidly validate.
  • STEM Education: Serves as a hands-on pedagogical tool demonstrating how infrared astronomy, proper motion, and planetary detection actually operate.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Frontend & Client Architecture:
    • HTML5 & CSS3: Semantic markup, CSS Grid, Flexbox, CSS Custom Properties (theming), and responsive breakpoints.
    • Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+): Zero external dependencies or build pipelines for maximum reliability and longevity.
    • HTML5 Canvas 2D API: Real-time procedural rendering of simulated starfields, point-spread functions (PSFs), motion vectors, and wipe curtains.
    • Browser Web APIs: localStorage for review persistence, Clipboard API for evidence sharing, and File API (URL.createObjectURL) for custom image loading.
    • Python 3.11+ / FastAPI (0.115.6) & Uvicorn: High-performance asynchronous REST API implementing scoring endpoints, IRSA link generators, and catalog lookups.
    • Pydantic: Robust data modeling and input boundary validation.
    • PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4: Spatial database schema utilizing spatial coordinates (GEOGRAPHY(POINT, 4326)), HEALPix sky indexing, and GiST indexes for efficient spatial queries.
    • Redis 7 & Docker Compose: Containerized deployment orchestrating API and database services with one command.
    • NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): SPHEREx spectral image query integration.
    • NASA JPL Small-Body Database (SBDB) REST API: Dynamic cross-matching to prevent re-flagging known asteroids and comets.
    • Astropy (Python): Reference pipeline standards for FITS header parsing and coordinate alignment.
  • AI Assistance: Anthropic’s Claude was utilized during development for code scaffolding, algorithm design, and documentation.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Modernizing a Classic Astronomical Instrument: Takes the 90-year-old analog blink comparator and transforms it into a digital, multi-epoch web workbench complete with real-time difference color-coding and continuous epoch scrubbing.
  • Directional Color Difference Mapping: Rather than simply showing dark or bright residual pixels, the difference engine highlights the earlier position in pink and the later position in blue, immediately communicating the direction and magnitude of the object's proper motion vector to the naked eye.
  • Gamified Onboarding: Integrates the "Spot the mover" challenge directly into the scientific tool, lowering the barrier to entry by turning complex astronomical anomaly detection into an intuitive skill-building game.
  • Standardized Evidence Dossier Generator: Features a one-click evidence clipboard exporter that formats candidate telemetry with strict scientific disclaimers, turning casual spotters into responsible citizen researchers.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Honesty vs. Hype: Faint objects in the outer Solar System (like a theoretical Planet X / Planet Nine) are exceptionally cold, distant, and dim; a single SPHEREx exposure may not have sufficient signal-to-noise for an immediate definitive detection. We explicitly labeled all built-in demonstration fields as simulated and engineered the tool around vetting leads rather than generating unverified claims.
  • Data Volume & Bandwidth Constraints: Full-resolution SPHEREx FITS exposures are large (often ~69 MB per file across multiple spectral bands). To prevent network bottlenecks and high compute costs, the app was designed around lightweight localized cutouts and client-side rendering.
  • Catalog Deconfliction: Recognizes that the vast majority of moving objects in infrared sky surveys are known Main-Belt asteroids, near-Earth objects, or variable stars. The system was structured to query the JPL Small-Body Database to rule out known objects early.
  • Reliability & Portability: By deliberately avoiding complex frontend frameworks (React/Vue) or heavy build dependencies, the entire core application can be emailed, downloaded, or run completely offline from a thumb drive anywhere in the world.
